title: Crime & Punishment: Stretch
welcome_lead: Evaluate the death penalty, hate crime and how religion guides justice in a modern multi-faith society.
meta_desc: GCSE RS Crime & Punishment stretch — evaluate the death penalty, hate crime and modern justice.
final_note: You can now construct evaluative arguments on punishment for top exam marks.

concepts.def: Crime motivated by prejudice (race, religion, sexuality)
Showing compassion when punishment is deserved
Treating people fairly according to right and wrong
Inner moral sense — what is right or wrong

walkthroughs.body_html:
For: retribution (Genesis 9:6), strong deterrent, permanent protection.

Against: innocent people executed, no chance to reform, breaks 'do not murder' (Exodus 20:13). Jesus stopped a stoning (John 8:7).

The Catholic Church now teaches it is 'inadmissible' (Catechism 2267, revised 2018).

Hate crime is crime motivated by prejudice. Both Christianity and Islam strictly forbid it.

Jesus: 'Love your neighbour as yourself' (Mark 12:31). Qur'an 49:13: 'We made you into nations and tribes that you may know one another.'

UK law treats prejudice as an aggravating factor in sentencing.

A central tension: justice demands punishment, mercy invites forgiveness.

Christianity holds them together at the cross — Jesus takes the punishment so sinners are forgiven (Romans 3:23-26).

Islam balances qisas (retaliation) with the higher reward for pardoning (Qur'an 5:45). A good evaluation question weighs both values.

mcqs.q: In which Gospel does Jesus say 'Let any one of you who is without sin be the first to throw a stone'?
Which Catechism paragraph (revised 2018) calls the death penalty 'inadmissible'?

numericals.q: Qur'an 49:13 says God made humans into nations and tribes for what reason? (Answer the surah number.)

free_texts.q: What single word means 'crime motivated by prejudice'? Two words allowed — give the first.
